venues.d: The capital's defining address — a Belle Époque palace beside the Prado, restored to its full 1910 grandeur.
Seven heritage buildings woven into one grand house at Canalejas — Four Seasons' first Spanish address, between Sol and the Prado.
The Salamanca grande dame reborn — Rosewood's flagship on Madrid's most coveted boulevard, all calm and quiet polish.
A contemporary luxury house on the Golden Mile, in the former Gran Hotel Velázquez — bold, design-led, and gastronomically serious.

venues.n: Santo Mauro, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.d: A duke's 1894 neoclassical mansion turned intimate palace hotel — a marble staircase, a garden, and deep quiet off the Castellana.
A restored 19th-century Salamanca townhouse turned intimate luxury hotel, on the city's smartest shopping street.

venues.n: Gran Meliá Palacio de los Duques
venues.d: A 19th-century palace and former 13th-century convent by the Royal Palace, dressed with a Velázquez-inspired hand.
Ian Schrager's cool, light-filled house in the old centre — a rooftop, a pool and a lively scene under one modern roof.
A restored Belle Époque palace turned boutique house between Chamberí and Chueca — a Natura Bissé spa and quiet good taste.
An early-20th-century building crowned by one of Madrid's great rooftops, at the head of Gran Vía.
A 1912 grand hotel between the Prado and the Thyssen — its stained-glass rotunda one of the city's great rooms.
Madrid's oldest luxury hotel, reborn — a jewel-box in the literary quarter, restored with real depth of character.
Philippe Starck's exuberant, botanical Madrid house — a lush, design-forward stay near the Salamanca boutiques.
A restored palace near Atocha and the Reina Sofía, with a rooftop pool over the old town.
A design-led townhouse in the heart of Chueca — warm, sociable and well-placed for the city's most vibrant quarter.
A polished, contemporary house near Atocha station and the Retiro — easy connections and a rooftop terrace.
Dabiz Muñoz's wild, world-beating three-star canvas — the most audacious tasting menu in Spain, and one of the greatest on earth.
Quique Dacosta's Mediterranean haute cuisine in the Ritz's Belle Époque splendour — two stars beside the Prado.
The Sandoval brothers' theatre of a restaurant — a five-act journey from cellar to kitchen to table, held at two stars.
Paco Roncero's avant-garde cooking inside the grand Casino de Madrid — technical, playful, two stars.
Diego Guerrero's raw, industrial-chic room and free-thinking cooking — one of Madrid's most personal two-star tables.
Dani García's fire-and-smoke haute cuisine — a small, intense counter built around the embers, at two stars.
Ramón Freixa's signature cooking, back at two stars in an intimate new atelier — precise, considered, personal.
Product-driven cooking of real refinement, and a live-fire counter that is a show in itself.
Rodrigo de la Calle's temple to the vegetable — 'gastrobotánica' cooking that puts produce centre-stage.
Grand, gracious service and classical-contemporary cooking — a room that revived the art of the trolley and the table-side flourish.

venues.a: Barrio de las Letras (Calle San Blas)
venues.d: A Japanese-Spanish counter and a hidden 'bunker' below — Julián Mármol's cult sushi and kaiseki.
Javi Estévez's ode to offal — the humblest cuts turned into something dazzling, and a star for the effort.
Marcos Granda's produce-led Mediterranean cooking and an exceptional cellar — a sommelier's restaurant.
A tiny, four-table gastronomic room inside the world's great flamenco tablao — dinner and pure flamenco in one night.
Javier Aranda's minimalist room around an open kitchen — precise, seasonal cooking under a striking geometric ceiling.
The godfather of Spanish-Japanese fusion — Ricardo Sanz's nigiri and Mediterranean-inflected sushi at the Wellington.
Dabiz Muñoz's dumpling house — the DiverXO imagination poured into pasta and dumplings from around the world.
Hugo Muñoz's free-wheeling Spanish-Japanese cooking — one of the city's most exciting recent stars.
A fish-house of extraordinary quality from a historic fishmonger — the finest seafood, treated with reverence.
Edwin Rodríguez's refined Colombian cooking — the first star for a kitchen bringing South America to Madrid.

venues.a: Centro (Hotel Urban, Carrera de San Jerónimo)
venues.d: Contemporary Spanish cooking with a Levantine hand, inside the design-led Hotel Urban.
Miguel Carretero's cooking rooted in the Spanish countryside — game, croquetas and produce done seriously.

venues.a: Barrio de las Letras (Calle Lope de Vega)
venues.d: Safe Cruz's tribute to Canary Islands cooking — a tiny room bringing the archipelago's produce and culture to Madrid.
A young couple's produce-led tasting menu by the river — tradition and innovation in a serene, out-of-the-way room.
Marcos Granda's intimate omakase counter — precise, seasonal Japanese cooking in a hushed, tiny room.
Óscar Velasco and Montse Abellá's market-driven cooking — a first star for two of Spain's most respected hands.
A beloved market-cuisine institution behind Gran Vía — Juanjo López's produce so good the menu changes by the morning.
The oldest restaurant on earth, open since 1725 — cochinillo and cordero from the original wood-fired oven.
Roberto Martínez Foronda's tiny market stall doing vivid Asian-Peruvian fusion — one of Madrid's most joyful tables.
A trio of chefs weaving Mediterranean, Japanese and Peruvian threads — creative, generous, always full.
Mario Payán's Japanese counter — an honest, affordable omakase and one of the city's best sushi seats for the price.
An old-fashioned Madrid tavern reborn — traditional Spanish cooking and a bar, done with real care.
Honest, vibrant Mexican cooking in the heart of Chueca — a Bib Gourmand favourite for good, affordable food.
Classic Spanish taberna cooking of the highest order — the tortilla and croquetas that locals argue are the city's best.

venues.a: Chamberí (Plaza del Descubridor Diego de Ordás)
venues.d: César Martín's warm, produce-led cooking — an inventive neighbourhood room that has kept its Bib for years.

Spain's crown jewel of a picture gallery: Velázquez's Las Meninas, Goya's Black Paintings and the largest hoard of Bosch and Titian anywhere. Book a private out-of-hours or expert-led tour so a multi-generational family can stand alone before the masterpieces before the crowds arrive.

venues.n: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía
venues.d: Home to Picasso's Guernica, which commands its own hushed room, alongside the country's greatest collection of Dalí and Miró. A private guide makes the modern-art narrative land for teenagers and grandparents alike.

The third point of the Golden Triangle, a former private aristocratic collection that fills the gaps the Prado and Reina Sofía leave — from early Italian gold-ground panels to Hopper and Impressionism. Its scale is human, ideal for a gentle, unhurried afternoon.

One of the largest palaces in Europe with over 3,000 rooms — grander than Versailles or Buckingham — where the Throne Room, Royal Armoury and Stradivarius collection dazzle. Private after-hours access can be arranged for discreet visits.

Madrid's neo-Gothic cathedral faces the Royal Palace across the Plaza de la Armería, its brightly coloured modern ceiling a surprise inside a classical shell. Climb to the dome for a quiet rooftop panorama over the old town.

The city's green lung and former royal pleasure garden, made for rowing on the boating lake, strolling shaded avenues and letting children run free. Its rose garden and grand monuments reward a slow morning walk.

A shimmering 1887 glass-and-iron pavilion set beside a pond in the Retiro, one of Madrid's most photographed structures. Note it is closed for restoration until around 2027, though its striking exterior — currently wrapped in Reina Sofía art interventions — is still worth the walk.

The grand arcaded 17th-century square at the heart of Habsburg Madrid, ringed by frescoed facades and framed by nine stone archways. Best at early morning or evening when the day-trippers thin and the porticoes empty out.

The symbolic centre of Spain, marked by the Kilometre Zero plaque from which all the country's roads are measured and the bear-and-strawberry-tree statue. A useful orienting point and the beating pulse of the city.

Madrid's early-20th-century grand boulevard of belle-époque and art-deco towers, cinemas and rooftop bars — the 'Spanish Broadway'. Walk it at dusk when the facades light up, or catch a Spanish-language musical.

A beautiful 1916 wrought-iron market turned gourmet food hall beside Plaza Mayor, where stalls run from Galician shellfish to Rodrigo de la Calle's Michelin-starred paella. Grazing here suits mixed groups and there are plenty of vegetable and cheese counters for veg-aware guests.

Spain's largest open-air flea market, spilling down La Latina's streets every Sunday morning with antiques, leather, prints and curios. Follow it with tapas and a vermouth in the surrounding taverns, a cherished local Sunday ritual.

A genuine 2nd-century-BC Egyptian temple, gifted to Spain and re-erected on a hill west of the centre, mirrored in a reflecting pool. It is Madrid's most romantic sunset spot, when the stones glow amber over the sierra.

venues.n: Azotea del Círculo de Bellas Artes
venues.d: The rooftop terrace of the century-old fine-arts club, 56 metres up, delivers a 360-degree sweep over Gran Vía, Cibeles and the tiled skyline. Come at golden hour with a cocktail for the most elegant view in the city.

Madrid's 1850 opera house, facing the Royal Palace, stages world-class opera and ballet under lavish gilt and superb acoustics. A private box turns an evening into an occasion for a family or a discreet party.

Widely regarded as the finest flamenco tablao in the world, hosting legendary dancers since 1956 in an intimate room where you dine as you watch. Its separate gastronomic space under chef David García holds a Michelin star — a rare pairing of art and haute cuisine.

Real Madrid's newly rebuilt cathedral of football, where the Bernabéu Tour walks you onto the pitch, through the dressing room and past the trophy room. A thrill for children and lifelong fans; VIP and matchday hospitality can be arranged discreetly.

Chef Dabiz Muñoz's boundary-smashing tasting menu is the only three-Michelin-star table in Madrid and ranks among the world's top five restaurants. A theatrical, once-in-a-trip splurge; the kitchen accommodates dietary requests with advance notice.

venues.n: Barrio de Salamanca — the Golden Mile
venues.d: Madrid's most refined district, where Calle Serrano and Calle Ortega y Gasset line up Loewe, Chanel, Dior and Spain's finest ateliers amid grand 19th-century mansions. The natural base for luxury shopping and elegant, unhurried lunches.

The preserved home, studio and Andalusian-inspired garden of Joaquín Sorolla, Spain's master of light, hung with over a thousand of his luminous canvases. A serene, intimate escape that feels worlds away from the tourist trail.

The former mansion of a financier-collector, four floors of Goya, El Greco, Zurbarán, jewellery and ivories displayed in opulent private-house rooms. One of Madrid's most rewarding hidden gems, rarely crowded.

A 19th-century aristocrat's palace frozen in time, its ballroom, chandeliers, tapestries and armour left exactly as the Marquis of Cerralbo arranged them. An intimate window into how Madrid's nobility once lived.

An 18th-century royal botanical garden of some 5,000 plant species right beside the Prado, laid out in tranquil terraces and glasshouses. A calming green interval between museum visits, easy for elders and children.

A still-working convent of Franciscan nuns founded in 1559 in a former royal palace, concealing an astonishing hoard of tapestries, paintings and a frescoed grand staircase. Guided visits only, which keeps this treasure blissfully quiet.

venues.n: Real Basílica de San Francisco el Grande
venues.d: A neoclassical basilica crowned by one of the largest domes in Europe, its interior a gilded blaze of frescoes and canvases including an early Goya. Underrated and often near-empty despite its splendour.

venues.n: Ermita de San Antonio de la Florida
venues.d: A tiny hermitage whose dome Goya frescoed in 1798 — and beneath which the painter himself is buried. A jewel-box of a stop, moving for anyone who has just seen his work in the Prado.

A Herzog & de Meuron arts centre appearing to float above the street, fronted by a living wall of 15,000 plants — the first vertical garden in Spain. Ambitious rotating exhibitions make it a reliable cultural draw beside the Golden Triangle.

The old haunt of Cervantes, Lope de Vega and Spain's Golden Age writers, now a lattice of pedestrian lanes with literary quotes underfoot, wine bars and antique shops. A characterful stroll between the Prado and Puerta del Sol.

Madrid's most atmospheric tapas district, its Cava Baja and Cava Alta streets packed with historic taverns pouring vermouth and plating croquetas and tortilla. Many kitchens do excellent vegetable and egg dishes, easy for veg-aware guests to graze happily.

The bohemian, design-forward barrio born of Madrid's 1980s countercultural Movida, now full of vintage boutiques, specialty coffee and independent galleries. A younger, creative counterpoint for teenagers and design lovers.

Madrid's stylish, welcoming and famously vibrant quarter, dense with concept stores, terraces and some of the city's best modern restaurants around Mercado de San Antón. Lively yet easy, with rooftop dining that suits mixed groups.

A 92-metre observation tower with a glass-walled deck giving a clean, elevated panorama over the western parks, the sierra and the whole city grid. A quick, uncrowded way to grasp Madrid's layout on arrival.

A vast former slaughterhouse reborn as a raw, buzzing contemporary-arts campus of cinemas, exhibition halls, design studios and theatre. A window into today's creative Madrid, and a striking piece of industrial reuse.

A riverside park reclaimed by burying the ring road, now a leafy ribbon of walkways, playgrounds and beach-fountains along the Manzanares. A relaxed, family-friendly counterpoint to the museums, best on foot or by bicycle.

venues.n: Plaza de Cibeles & Palacio de Cibeles rooftop
venues.d: The city's most iconic fountain and civic square, with the wedding-cake CentroCentro palace beside it offering a viewing terrace, Mirador Madrid, over the rooftops. The junction of the Paseo del Prado's grand ceremonial axis.

venues.n: Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando
venues.d: A superb, blessedly quiet picture gallery holding Goyas — including his own self-portraits — plus Zurbarán, Rubens and El Greco, where the great painter once served as director. The connoisseur's alternative to the Prado's crowds.

venues.n: El Corte Inglés Gourmet Experience, Callao
venues.d: A top-floor food hall and terrace with a head-on view of the Gran Vía's illuminated Schweppes building and rooftops. Casual, high-energy and easy for a mixed-age group wanting a drink with a view.

Spain's national archaeology museum, whose star is the enigmatic Iberian sculpture the Lady of Elche, alongside Roman mosaics and Visigothic treasures. Beautifully modernised and rarely overwhelming — good for curious children.

venues.a: Day trip — approx. 70 km / 35 min by high-speed train
venues.d: A medieval hilltop city encircled by the Tagus where Christian, Muslim and Jewish worlds fused, home to El Greco's greatest works and a soaring Gothic cathedral. A private guide and car make an unforgettable full day; its whole historic city is a UNESCO site.

venues.a: Day trip — approx. 90 km / 30 min by high-speed train
venues.d: A storybook town crowned by a Roman aqueduct of 20,000 mortar-free granite blocks and the turreted Alcázar that inspired Disney. Lunch on the region's famed roast — or lighter Castilian fare for veg-aware guests — before the drive back.

venues.n: El Escorial (Real Monasterio de San Lorenzo)
venues.d: Philip II's austere granite monastery-palace at the foot of the sierra, part royal mausoleum, part library, part basilica, and one of Spain's most powerful monuments. Cool mountain air and a grand setting make it an easy, rewarding half-day.

A royal spring retreat of palaces and formal riverside gardens along the Tagus, all fountains, tree-lined avenues and 18th-century calm. Arrive on the vintage Strawberry Train in season for a gentle, multi-generational outing.

The world's first planned university city and Cervantes's birthplace, with a golden-stone historic quarter and Spain's most storied lecture halls. A cultured, easy escape that pairs literary heritage with excellent Castilian tapas.

A perfectly preserved medieval town built around a circular, galleried Plaza Mayor that doubles as a bullring, ringed by taverns pouring the local anís. A charming, off-the-beaten-track lunch stop far from the crowds.
Madrid's globally-ranked cocktail bar — Diego Cabrera's high-energy, comic-book den of bold, laboratory-made drinks.
A dual wine bar and cocktail lab from the Villalón brothers — 500 labels upstairs, farm-to-glass drinks below.
The rooftop of Madrid's grand 1880s arts club — the definitive panorama over Gran Vía and the Metropolis dome.
A sleek rooftop over the theatre-lit canyon of Gran Vía — cocktails with the city's grandest avenue at your feet.
A twelfth-floor rooftop and pool over Plaza de España — cocktails with the Royal Palace and Sierra beyond.
An Art Deco cocktail bar in a duke's mansion, channelling old New York — the most discreet drink in the city.
The EDITION's buzzy rooftop over the old centre — a pool, a scene and a considered drink under the Madrid sky.
A polished cocktail bar inside the Four Seasons at Canalejas — expert drinks in the city's finest new luxury house.
